Desktop DAWs and visual engines require manual mouse interactions, proprietary project files, and heavy graphical interfaces that agents cannot operate. Infinite bridges this gap by exposing its entire C++20 engine through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and a dedicated Python SDK . The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool. It reads a plain-text patch and writes stills, video and audio, with no window and no mouse. A patch is text, so an agent such as Claude can write it, check it, listen to it and fix it in a loop. This post shows that loop, then three small patches: a sound, a picture and a 3D scene. It builds on the headless render walkthrough and the Headless User Guide . Why a text patch suits an agent Most creative tools hide their state behind a window. An agent can only guess at what a click did. An Infinite patch is different in four ways: It is text. A patch is a list of node , cable , mod and expr lines in a .inf file. An agent writes it the way it writes code, and it diffs cleanly in version control. The engine explains itself. Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with defaults, ranges and dropdown options, so the agent never has to guess a name or a range. Errors are specific. --validate reports every problem with a line number and a hint that names the nearest valid key. Results are machine readable. The last line printed is one JSON object with ok , files , warnings and errors , and the exit code says whether the patch loaded, was refused or failed to render. The output is also deterministic: the same patch gives the same frames and the same samples, so an agent can change one thing and trust that any difference came from that change. The loop an agent follows The Headless User Guide gives the order, and it works as a prompt for an agent as it stands: Describe. Ask the engine for the node's controls with --describe . Do not guess. Write the smallest patch that could work. Leave every control you do not change at its default. Validate with --validate until the exit code is 0. Explain with --explain , which prints the graph that was actually built. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch, so the agent compares this against what you asked for. Look and listen. --frame draws stills and --audio-summary describes the sound as numbers. Fix one thing at a time and go back to step 3. Render the final file with --render . Infinite ships this loop as an agent skill, infinite-patch-authoring , written for AI coding agents. Point your agent at it and at the Headless User Guide, then describe what you want. First identified in computer science by E. Bjorklund in 2003 for timing neutron accelerators at Los Alamos, and brought into music theory by Godfried Toussaint in 2005, Euclidean rhythms revealed a startling truth: the mathematical distribution of pulses on a circle generates the foundational rhythmic structures of traditional music worldwide. In modern modular synthesis and creative coding environments like Infinite , Euclidean sequencers provide an elegant alternative to static step grids. Because the pattern emerges directly from two integer parameters, pulse count and step length, composers can morph complex groove structures live without editing step arrays by hand. Here is how the mathematics work, how to implement the algorithm in a single line of procedural code, and how to patch Euclidean triggers into synthesizers and 3D geometry simultaneously. Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithm diagram showing geometric hit distributions and modular node patching From nuclear accelerators to world rhythms The core challenge of rhythmic distribution can be stated simply: given $n$ available steps in a bar and $k$ active beats, how can we space the beats so the interval between any two consecutive hits differs by at most one step? Bjorklund originally developed an iterative algorithm based on Euclid's greatest common divisor method. Starting with a set of $k$ ones (active hits) and $n - k$ zeros (rests), the algorithm repeatedly distributes the smaller group into remainder sequences until no division remains. When applied to musical intervals, Toussaint observed that this mechanical reduction produces virtually every major non-Western and folk timeline pattern: E(3, 8) produces [X . . X . . X .] , the Cuban tresillo and Caribbean habanera rhythm. E(5, 8) produces [X . X X . X X .] , the Cuban cinquillo and Spanish tango. E(5, 12) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X .] , the Venda clapping pattern from South Africa. E(7, 12) produces [X . X . X X . X . X . X] , the West African bell pattern (Bembe), which is also geometrically isomorphic to the diatonic major scale on a twelve-tone chromatic circle. E(5, 16) produces [X . . X . . X . . . X . . X . .] , the Brazilian bossa nova necklace. E(7, 16) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X . . X . .] , a fundamental Brazilian samba rhythm. Because each pattern can be rotated around the circular step circle, a single pair of integers yields multiple distinct syncopations simply by advancing the starting step index. The closed-form integer Bresenham formula While Bjorklund's recursive array partitioning works well for static sequence generation, running recursive string manipulations inside a real-time audio thread or graphics shader is inefficient. Fortunately, Euclidean distribution can be expressed in closed form as a one-dimensional Bresenham line-drawing algorithm. Imagine drawing a continuous line from coordinate (0, 0) to (n, k) on a 2D integer grid. Each time the line crosses an integer threshold on the vertical axis, an active hit occurs. A Blur node blurs and a Delay node delays. Creative work often needs something in between, so Infinite includes Field , a kernel language for shaders, geometry and audio: a small language for writing what a node does. One idea: a kernel run once per element A Field node runs your kernel once for every element of its domain, forever. The domain is chosen by the node, not by you: col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5) // once per pixel, on the GPU: a shader P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 // once per point in a mesh: a geometry deformer out = in * gain // once per audio sample: a DSP effect You never declare a backend. The same way of thinking covers pictures, shapes and sound. The Field nodes Node Domain What it does Field Pixel pixel Per-pixel kernel compiled to GLSL, with state cells for feedback Field Modifier element Per-vertex kernel over existing geometry Field Primitive element Generates point geometry such as spirals, lattices and torus knots Field Effect sample Per-sample audio effect with in , out , state and param Field Synth sample A polyphonic synth voice driven by freq and gate Field Notes sample Sends notes with note(pitch, vel, len) and reads the transport Field Graph graph Runs at edit time and builds real nodes and cables Knobs that become pins A kernel can declare parameters in its own code, and each one becomes a real input on the node: param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99] state float z = 0 z += (in - z) * cutoff out = z That is a one-pole low-pass filter. The cutoff pin can be wired to an LFO, a MIDI knob or the output of an Audio Analyze node like any other control, and it survives save and load. Why a language, not another plugin format A kernel is short enough to read in one go and to share as a text file. How we tested Everything ran on a base MacBook Air with an Apple M2 and 8 GB of memory, on macOS, between 12 and 17 October 2026. That is the cheapest model on purpose: if it is fast there, it is fast on yours. Nothing was measured on Windows or Linux. The tests treat every product as a black box. Notes or a test signal go in, and what comes out is measured. Competitor plugins run inside Infinite's own plugin host, with default settings and no hand-picked presets, and the same code measures them as measures Infinite's own nodes. The tools are in the repository under tools/re-survey , so you can repeat any of it. The good news Launch: 0.34 seconds from launch to first frame. Opening a 400-node patch takes 6 ms. Footprint: 244 MB of memory with the app open and idle, and a 45 MB download. That is less memory than Ableton Live (672 MB), Blender (693 MB), Bitwig (1,392 MB) and TouchDesigner (1,396 MB) in the same idle test. Synth accuracy: The Wavetable synth has a worst pitch error of 0.2 cents across the keyboard. Vital and Serum 2 measure the same. Off-note energy stays between about -81 and -85 dB, even at the top of the keyboard where cheap synths alias. Synth cost: The Wavetable synth uses 1.45 ms of CPU per second of audio for each voice. Vital uses 2.82 ms and Serum 2 uses 3.23 ms. Video export: On matched test scenes, Infinite exported ProRes 4444 at 170 frames a second at 720p and 44 at 4K. Blender managed 1.6 and 0.5. These are different renderers, so this compares throughput, not image style. Plugins: 97.6 % of the plugins installed on the test machine load and pass audio in Infinite's plugin host. Live use: zero audio dropouts and zero missed screen refreshes in the standard live-performance test. Where Infinite is behind We list these on the report as below target: Idle CPU: With nothing loaded, Infinite sits at 12.3 % of one core. Logic, Blender and Vital sit under 4 %. Built-in effects: The EQ, Limiter, Drive and Chorus cost more CPU than the plugin equivalents. Instancing: 10,000 instanced objects cost 3.1 ms a frame in Infinite and 1.3 ms in Blender. Heavy projector scenes: The heaviest test (four 4K videos, three output windows, a camera and Syphon at once) drops frames. Normal and 1080p scenes do not. Default levels: Reverb, Delay, Chorus and Flanger come out louder than they go in at their default settings. What the numbers do not say One laptop is one data point. The comparisons are about throughput and cost under a fixed test, not about taste: a faster export does not make a better picture, and equal pitch accuracy does not make two synths sound alike. In practice, embedding real-time generative computer graphics on the web usually means pulling in large third-party runtime bundles, wrangling WebAudio permission policies, managing asset loading cascades, and debugging WebGL canvas resize glitches across mobile viewports. Infinite approaches web graphics from a different perspective. Because Infinite compiles procedural fragment shaders, JavaScript sketches, and per-sample audio DSP nodes into self-contained formats, its web export pipeline generates standalone HTML widgets that require zero external dependencies, zero CDN requests, and zero script frameworks. Here is how these embeds are structured, how the microphone reactivity works, and how you can place one on any page with a standard iframe. The problem with traditional web audio visualisers Most web visualisers rely on heavy JavaScript libraries such as Three.js, Babylon.js, or complex bundling setups. When embedded inside an article or project portfolio, these libraries create three distinct friction points: Payload weight and cold starts : Loading megabyte-scale runtime libraries introduces layout shifts, slow paint times, and stuttering initial frames. In traditional generative art, procedural movement often relies on periodic functions like sine waves or pseudorandom noise fields. While periodic functions offer predictable repetition and noise fields produce uncorrelated drifting, neither captures the natural tension of complex physical systems: structured form that evolves continuously without ever repeating. In modular workstations like Infinite , the Lorenz attractor bridges mathematics, real-time computer graphics, and modular sound design. By evaluating its three coupled differential equations inside a programmable canvas, artists can project intricate three-dimensional phase space paths, modulate attractor dynamics live with audio frequencies, and sonify chaotic coordinates into synthesiser parameters. Here is how the underlying non-linear mathematics work, how to implement the simulation inside a Sketch node, and how to patch chaotic variables across visual and audio nodes on a single canvas. Lorenz attractor interactive simulation diagram displaying differential equations, phase space trajectories, and modular node wiring The geometry of deterministic chaos The Lorenz system was introduced in 1963 by mathematician and meteorologist Edward Lorenz. While studying a simplified twelve-variable mathematical model of atmospheric convection, Lorenz reduced the convective fluid flow between warm lower and cool upper boundaries to a minimal system of three autonomous ordinary differential equations: dx / dt = sigma * (y - x) dy / dt = x * (rho - z) - y dz / dt = x * y - beta * z Here, the state variables describe idealized physical properties: x is proportional to the rate of convective fluid circulation. y is proportional to the horizontal temperature variation between ascending and descending currents. z measures the distortion of the vertical temperature profile from pure linearity. The three system parameters govern the physical regime: sigma (the Prandtl number) represents the ratio of kinematic viscosity to thermal diffusivity. In standard simulations, this is fixed at 10.0 . beta represents the geometric aspect ratio of the convective roll cells, traditionally set to 8.0 / 3.0 (approximately 2.667 ). rho (the Rayleigh number) measures the normalized temperature difference driving the fluid convection. It serves as the primary bifurcation parameter. When rho is less than 1.0 , the system has only one stable equilibrium at the coordinate origin (0, 0, 0) , representing pure conduction where fluid motion dissipates. As rho exceeds 1.0 , two symmetric convective fixed points emerge, labelled C+ and C- : C+, C- = (+-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), +-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), rho - 1) At the canonical threshold rho = 28.0 , both equilibrium points become unstable spirals. Instead of settling into a fixed point or a simple limit cycle, the trajectory enters bounded deterministic chaos. The path orbits one fixed point, spirals outward as its radius expands, and then crosses the saddle point at the origin to loop around the opposing lobe. Your code runs on the audio thread once per sample (48,000 times per second), compiled to a register machine that executes with zero memory allocations. How the sample register machine works When you place a Field Synth ( Synths Field Synth ) or Field Effect ( AudioEffects Field Effect ) node, Infinite compiles the kernel expression to a compact bytecode representation that evaluates on register cells. Built-in variables available on the audio thread sr : Audio sample rate in Hz (typically 48000.0 ). in : Incoming audio sample value ( [-1.0, 1.0] ) in Field Effect. out : Output audio sample to write. freq : Note frequency in Hz (voice pitch in Field Synth). gate : 1.0 while a MIDI note is held down, 0.0 when released. noteVel : Key velocity ( [0.0, 1.0] ). state : Declares per-voice persistent memory preserved across samples. param : Exposes a modulatable float knob on the node body with min/max bounds. A 1-pole lowpass filter kernel Here is a classic 1-pole lowpass filter written in 4 lines: param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99] state float z = 0 z += (in - z) * cutoff out = z Because state float z = 0 allocates a persistent cell in the voice register, z retains its previous sample value, creating an analog RC filter response. Shipped Moog 4-pole ladder filter For aggressive saturation and self-oscillation, Infinite ships with a 4-pole cascaded non-linear filter: param float cutoff = 2200.0 [80.0, 14000.0] param float res = 0.70 [0.0, 0.98] param float drive = 1.50 [1.0, 4.0] param float mix = 1.0 [0.0, 1.0] state float s1 = 0 state float s2 = 0 state float s3 = 0 state float s4 = 0 f = clamp((cutoff / sr) * 2.2, 0.005, 0.42) feedback = (s4 * res * 3.6) / (1.0 + abs(s4) * 0.8) u = (in * drive) - feedback sat = u / (1.0 + abs(u) * 0.3) s1 = s1 + f * (sat - s1) s2 = s2 + f * (s1 - s2) s3 = s3 + f * (s2 - s3) s4 = s4 + f * (s3 - s4) wet = s4 out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix Notice the dry/wet mix pattern at the end: every Field audio effect ends with out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix , giving you instant parallel processing. Real-time mod matrix integration Unlike fixed DSP plugins, a Field Effect node can publish meter readings back to the visual and modulation canvas using reduce.rms : param float boost = 1.5 [0.5, 4.0] output frame float bass = reduce.rms(in, 20.0, 200.0) out = in * boost The bass scalar automatically becomes a second output pin on the node. You can run a cable from that pin directly into a 3D geometry deformer, a light intensity slider, or a GLSL shader. Most DAWs and visual tools only run with a window and a mouse. Infinite's engine does not need either. The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool, so a patch can be validated, drawn and rendered from a terminal, a script or a CI job. This post walks through the loop from the Headless User Guide : describe, write, validate, explain, look and listen, render. What you need The Infinite app. There is no separate package; the executable inside the app is the tool. A machine with working OpenGL, because frames are drawn by the real GPU pipeline. On Linux, a virtual display. Run each render as xvfb-run -a Infinite ... . A text editor. Patches are plain text files ending in .inf . Patches that use a camera, microphone or MIDI device are refused in headless mode (exit code 4), since there is no hardware to read. Swap them for a file or a generator. A complete patch in a dozen lines Save this as hello.inf : infinite-patch 1 node 1 Source Shape id shape i shapeType Star end node 2 Modulators LFO id lfo end node 3 Utility Output id out end cable out 0 shape mod shape sizeX lfo 0 0 1 0.5 expr shape rotation sin(t) * 90 That is one shape, one LFO and an output. The LFO drives the shape's width, and an expression spins it. Validate, draw, render Infinite --validate hello.inf Infinite --frame hello.inf 0,1,2 pics/ --contact-sheet sheet.png Infinite --render hello.inf hello.mp4 --duration 4 --fps 30 --validate loads the file strictly and lists every problem with its line number. --frame draws stills at 0, 1 and 2 seconds plus one labelled contact sheet. --render writes the video. Ask the engine, do not guess Two commands save a lot of trial and error: Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with their defaults, ranges and dropdown options. Infinite --explain hello.inf prints the graph that was actually built, so you can check every wire. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch. Measure the sound --audio-summary describes the audio as numbers: loudness, peaks, clipping, silence, a spectrum and a tempo guess. Infinite --audio-summary hello.inf summary.json --wav out.wav --duration 4 Add --stems id,id --stems-dir dir to write one WAV per named node, or --output node to measure a single Audio Out instead of the whole mix. Reading the result The last line printed is always one JSON object with ok , mode , frames , fps , size , audio , elapsed_ms , files , warnings and errors . A script can parse that line and branch on ok without scraping log text. Where this is useful Regression tests for sound and picture. Render a corpus of patches on every commit and compare the summaries. Batch exports. Produce a hundred variations of a piece from one patch with --set node.param=value . Bots and servers. But getting a Shadertoy shader to respond dynamically to your music, sync with MIDI, or render out to high-resolution MP4 video often involves clumsy workarounds, browser recording extensions, or complex OSC bridges. In Infinite, shaders are native first-class nodes that sit directly alongside polyphonic synthesizers, audio effects, and sequencers on one infinite canvas. The coordinate space mapping Shadertoy uses standard pixel coordinates: void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) { vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy; // ... } In Infinite's Field Pixel node ( Source FieldPixel ), coordinates are normalized and aspect-corrected by default: uv : normalized texture coordinate ( [0, 1] x [0, 1] ) aspect : screen width divided by screen height ( res.x / res.y ) t : elapsed time in seconds (equivalent to iTime ) p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect : centre-origin aspect-corrected coordinates Adding instant audio reactivity On Shadertoy, audio reactivity requires binding an audio texture input ( iChannel0 ). In Infinite, audio reactivity is immediate and native: Wire an Audio Analyze node to your incoming sound or synth output. The node exposes 8 spectral bands: sub-bass, bass, low-mid, mid, high-mid, presence, brilliance, and onset pulses. Wire any band pin directly into a parameter on your Field Pixel shader node. Here is an authentic audio-reactive neon tunnel kernel in Field language: p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect; r = length(p); a = atan(p.y, p.x); u_coord = a / 3.14159265; v_coord = 1.0 / (r + 0.001) + t * (1.5 + 1.2 * bass); grid_u = abs(fract(u_coord * 4.0) - 0.5); grid_v = abs(fract(v_coord * 2.0) - 0.5); lines = smoothstep(0.42, 0.49, max(grid_u, grid_v)); wire = vec3(lines) * vec3(0.1, 0.85, 1.0) * (0.8 + 0.6 * mid); center = vec3(0.95, 0.2, 0.6) * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.6, r)) * (0.8 + 0.8 * bass); col = (wire + center) * (0.7 + 0.5 * bass); Live interactive WebGL widget You can test this exact visualizer running live in WebGL below: powered by infinite by naman soni Exporting high-resolution video headlessly Unlike web tools that drop frames during screen capture, Infinite renders every single frame deterministically through its headless C++ engine: # Render a 1080p 60fps MP4 video with synced 24-bit audio ./Infinite --render /path/to/shader_patch.inf output.mp4 --duration 10 --fps 60 Every frame is rendered offscreen using OpenGL 3.2 framebuffers, guaranteeing zero dropped frames even on complex raymarchers. CHAPTER 01 What Field is, and why it exists Infinite is a node-based

CHAPTER 01 What Field is, and why it exists Infinite is a node-based audiovisual workstation: you build patches by wiring boxes together on a canvas. Most boxes do one fixed thing. Field is different. It is a small text language that lets you write what a box does, instead of picking from a menu. The one idea underneath all of Field is the kernel: a short body of code run once per element of some domain, automatically, forever. Write col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5) and it runs once per pixel, 60 times a second, on the GPU: a shader. Write P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 and it runs once per point in a mesh: a geometry deformer. Write out = in * 0.5 and it runs once per audio sample: a DSP effect. You never say where it runs; Field infers that from which identifiers your code touches. Every example in this manual is valid, runnable Field code written against the six node types that ship in Infinite today. Chapter 13 covers the language additions that landed after v1. CHAPTER 03 Core syntax Field reads like a small C-family language.

CHAPTER 03 Core syntax Field reads like a small C-family language. Here is everything that is not obvious from that alone. Bare names, no sigil Every identifier, whether a reserved name like P , uv , in , out or your own param , state and attrib names, is written bare, exactly like a normal variable. Unlike Houdini VEX's @P style, Field has no sigil at all. P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 Types and swizzles The type keywords are float , int , bool , vec2 , vec3 , vec4 . There is no string type inside a kernel body. Swizzles work like GLSL: .x .y .z .w and .r .g .b .a , one to four letters. The two letter sets do not mix in one swizzle ( .xg is not valid; use .xy or .rg ). Operators, comments and broadcast Arithmetic is + - * / % , comparison is < <= > >= == != , boolean is && || ! , and ^ is exponentiation ( a ^ b is pow(a, b) ), not XOR. There are no bitwise operators. // starts a line comment. A scalar auto-broadcasts against a vector: P += 0.1 adds to every component, with no vec3(0

CHAPTER 04 Declarations: attrib, param, state Three keywords cover everything a kernel needs to remember or expose: a per-element scratch value, a UI knob, and a value that reads back one cycle late. attrib: a value that lives per element Declares a per-element scratch value, initialized once. Whatever you assign into it that frame is what the rest of the kernel body sees. Element domain only. attrib float heat = 0 heat = (P.y + 1.0) * 0.5 Cd = vec3(heat, 0.2, 1.0 - heat) An element attribute ramp driving vertex colour. param: a value that becomes a UI knob param <type> <name> = <default> [<lo>, <hi>] declares a real, modulatable knob. It shows up on the node's faceplate, can be dragged, automated and cabled to a modulator. param float speed = 2.0 [0.1, 10.0] Punctuation: in pixel kernels every statement ends with a semicolon ( param float speed = 2.0 [0.1, 10.0]; ). CHAPTER 07 Randomness rand , noise and sh are pure functions of their arguments: same inputs, same output, always, so a kernel stays deterministic and re-runnable. There is no hidden global RNG state to seed or reset. rand(min, max, speed, seed) Takes 0 to 4 arguments; fewer arguments fall back to sane defaults. n = rand(0, 1, 2.0, 0) P += N * (n - 0.5) * 0.2 Normal displacement using smooth noise: 0 to 1, speed 2.0, seed 0. noise and sh noise and sh follow the same pure-function pattern as rand , taking 0 to 4 arguments. Reach for rand first for most device work; use noise or sh when you want a smoother or shaped variant and want to compare results by ear or eye. FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL INFINITE / FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL

CHAPTER 10 Device faceplate Every Field node has two views: a compact body on the canvas, and a separate editor window for the code. The compact node body shows the auto-generated param knobs, notice text and an "Edit Field..." button. No source code is visible here. The floating editor window, opened by "Edit Field...", is where you read and write the kernel's text, inspect compilation status and see a live preview. BEFORE YOU START What even is Infinite? Infinite is a node-based studio for making sound and image at the same time. Instead of separate apps for music, visuals, and 3D, you drop blocks called nodes onto one canvas and connect them with cables: a synth feeding a filter, a shape feeding a kaleidoscope, a drumbeat feeding a bouncing particle field.
